Yes. Several papers suggest machine learning can help detect very early dementia-related impairment, especially mild cognitive impairment and early Alzheimer’s disease [1,2,3,6,7,8,9]. They use different signals: clinical, neuropsychological, and neuroimaging measures for early Alzheimer’s detection [1]; video, audio, and text from naturalistic interactions to distinguish MCI from healthy aging [2,3]; speech and linguistic features as early markers of cognitive decline [4,6]; MRI and PET imaging for MCI and AD classification [8]; EEG for classifying MCI and dementia-related conditions [9]; and longitudinal clinical notes for dementia prognosis [5].

The papers differ mainly in setting and modality. Some target contactless or home-based screening using multimodal behavior or speech [2,3,6], while others focus on clinical imaging or records [1,5,8,9]. One speech study emphasizes multilingual Alzheimer’s detection across languages [4]. Overall, these results support ML as a useful aid for first-stage detection, though the abstracts do not show that it is sufficient on its own for diagnosis.
